summary: One of the documents that together define the Internet Printing Protocol (IPP). This one describes how IPP requests and responses are encoded and carried over HTTP. It is a standards-track document. It was replaced by RFC 8010.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2910 defines the binary encoding and HTTP transport for Internet Printing Protocol operations. It specifies how a request identifies a printer or job and how its attributes and optional document data are carried.

questions: how does ipp work over http
subtitle: How IPP/1.1 operations are encoded and transported over HTTP.

tldr.problem: The IPP model defines printing operations, but clients and printers also need a shared byte encoding and a way to carry requests and responses.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2910 encodes each operation as a binary message with tagged attributes and sends it as an application/ipp body in an HTTP/1.1 POST request or response. It also defines the ipp URL scheme for printers and jobs.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2910 obsoletes RFC 2565 and was itself obsoleted by RFC 8010. It was also updated by RFCs 3380, 3381, 3382, 3510, 3995, and 7472.

today: RFC 2910 was obsoleted by RFC 8010 and updated by RFC 3380, RFC 3381, RFC 3382, RFC 3510, RFC 3995, and RFC 7472. RFC 8010 is the later encoding and transport specification.

sections.title: The Operation and Transport Layers
sections.content:
RFC 2910 is part of a set of documents that define the Internet Printing Protocol (IPP). It describes two layers: an operation message in the body of an HTTP request or response, and the HTTP transport that carries the message. The IPP model document defines what the operations mean; this RFC defines their encoding and transport.

IPP/1.1 uses HTTP/1.1, but the two version numbers are independent. The operation body uses the media type application/ipp, and an operation message contains one IPP request or response.
sections.plainLanguage: IPP uses an operation message inside an HTTP message. This RFC explains how to encode the operation and carry it over HTTP.

sections.title: The Binary Operation Message
sections.content:
An IPP operation begins with a two-byte version number, a two-byte operation identifier or response status code, and a four-byte request identifier. It can then contain attribute groups, followed by exactly one end-of-attributes tag and optional document data. The IPP/1.1 version is encoded as %x01.01.

Attribute groups begin with delimiter tags. Each attribute has a value tag, a name length, a name, a value length, and a value. Additional values for the same attribute use a zero name length. Integer fields use signed, two's-complement big-endian encoding, and the tag identifies the type of each attribute value.
sections.plainLanguage: The message has fixed opening fields, tagged attribute groups, and a marker that ends the attributes. Optional document data follows that marker.

sections.title: Carrying IPP over HTTP
sections.content:
Every HTTP operation uses POST, and both the request and response use application/ipp as the content type. An IPP printer must support HTTP over port 631. HTTP servers must support chunked IPP requests, and IPP clients must support chunked responses.

The target printer or job appears in the HTTP request URI and in an IPP operation attribute. The two URIs must identify the same object, although one may be relative and the other absolute. The URI inside the operation must be absolute. The printer does not have to check whether the two targets match.
sections.plainLanguage: An IPP request is sent as an HTTP POST with an IPP body. The printer or job is identified both in the HTTP request and in an attribute inside that body.

sections.title: The ipp URL Scheme
sections.content:
The ipp URL scheme identifies an IPP printer or job. It represents a print service and uses port 631 by default. Because the HTTP layer does not use the ipp scheme, a client changes it to http for the HTTP request and adds port 631 if the URL has no explicit port.

The client keeps the original ipp URL in the IPP operation attribute while using the converted HTTP URL in the HTTP request line and headers. A printer that registers its URL with a directory service must register an ipp URL.
sections.plainLanguage: The ipp URL identifies a printer or job. The client converts it for HTTP transport but keeps the ipp URL in the operation message.

sections.title: Authentication and Transport Security
sections.content:
The IPP model identifies client authentication, server authentication, and operation privacy as security needs. IPP clients must support HTTP Digest Authentication, while printers should support it. Printers should support TLS for server authentication and operation privacy; TLS may also be used for client authentication.

If a printer or client supports TLS, it must support the cipher suite TLS_DHE_DSS_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA. IPP uses the HTTP Upgrade mechanism to begin TLS, so the initial IPP request is sent before the TLS switch. A lower version number or a non-secure URL scheme must not be used to weaken security.
sections.plainLanguage: Authentication can help confirm the client and server, and TLS can protect operations from eavesdropping. A client must not be able to weaken security by requesting an older version or non-secure URL.
